name: Quadrantid Meteor Shower
description: Short, sharp peak lasting only ~6 hours. Often overlooked due to cold January nights and narrow peak window. Blue meteors, medium speed.

name: Lyrid Meteor Shower
description: One of the oldest recorded meteor showers — observed for 2,700 years. Typically modest rates but occasional outbursts. Fast, bright meteors with persistent trains.

name: Eta Aquariid Meteor Shower
description: Debris from Halley's Comet! Very fast meteors — the fastest of all annual showers. Best viewed from southern latitudes (India is well-positioned). Radiant is low, so meteors have long, dramatic trails across the sky.

name: Perseid Meteor Shower
description: The most popular meteor shower — reliable, prolific, and happens during warm summer nights. Fast, bright meteors with frequent fireballs. Radiant is high in the sky from India during peak hours.

name: Orionid Meteor Shower
description: The second shower from Halley's Comet each year. Fast meteors, often with persistent green/yellow trains. Modest rates but worth watching — you're seeing Halley's legacy.

name: Leonid Meteor Shower
description: Famous for historic meteor storms (1833, 1966, 2001 — thousands per hour). In normal years, rates are modest. The fastest meteors of any major shower at 71 km/s — blink and you'll miss them. Bright fireballs possible.

name: Geminid Meteor Shower
description: The king of meteor showers. Highest reliable rates of any annual shower. Unlike most showers, activity starts early evening (radiant rises by 7 PM). Slow, bright, multi-colored meteors — white, yellow, green, blue. Uniquely sourced from an asteroid, not a comet.

name: Jupiter at Opposition
viewing_direction: E (rises at sunset, highest at midnight)
description: Jupiter at its closest and brightest for 2026. Visible all night long. Through binoculars, its 4 Galilean moons are clearly visible as tiny dots flanking the planet. Through a small telescope (even 60mm), cloud bands and the Great Red Spot become visible.

name: Saturn at Opposition
viewing_direction: E (rises at sunset, highest at midnight)
description: Saturn at its closest and brightest. The rings are visible through any telescope at 30x or more — a life-changing first sight for many observers. Ring tilt is currently decreasing — by 2025 they appear nearly edge-on. 2026 offers a slightly wider view.

name: Mars at Opposition
viewing_direction: E (rises at sunset, highest at midnight)
description: Mars at its closest approach since 2022. Bright reddish-orange, unmistakable to the naked eye. Through a telescope at 100x+, surface features (dark markings, polar ice cap) become visible. Best opposition until 2028.

name: Venus at Greatest Eastern Elongation
description: Venus at maximum angular distance from the Sun — visible as the brilliant 'evening star' for hours after sunset. Brightest object in the sky after the Sun and Moon. Through a telescope, Venus shows a clear half-phase (like a miniature half-moon).

name: Total Lunar Eclipse
viewing_direction: W (Moon setting during eclipse for India)
description: Total lunar eclipse — the Moon turns deep red ('Blood Moon') as Earth's shadow falls on it. From India, only the early partial phases may be visible before moonset. Western India has a slightly better view than eastern India.

name: Partial Solar Eclipse (visible from India)
description: A partial solar eclipse visible from much of India. The Moon will cover a portion of the Sun's disk. NEVER look at the Sun without proper solar filters — even during an eclipse. Solar eclipse glasses (ISO 12312-2 certified) are essential.

name: Milky Way Core Season
viewing_direction: S to SE (galactic center in Sagittarius)
best_hours: post-midnight (varies by month — center rises later in spring, earlier in summer)
description: The Milky Way's bright central bulge — the galactic center — is visible from March through October. Peak visibility is June–August when it arcs high overhead. Requires Bortle 4 or darker skies. From India, the galactic center passes almost directly overhead — one of the best viewing geometries on Earth.
